clinicalPearls: X-linked disorder caused by HSD17B10 (formerly HADH2) variants; the encoded protein is bifunctional, acting in isoleucine catabolism and as an essential subunit (MRPP2) of mitochondrial RNase P required for processing of mitochondrial transfer RNAs.

Urine organic acids classically show raised 2-methyl-3-hydroxybutyrate and tiglylglycine, but 2-methylacetoacetate is characteristically not elevated, which discriminates it from beta-ketothiolase (T2/ACAT1) deficiency.
Clinical severity does not correlate with residual dehydrogenase activity; the neurodegenerative phenotype tracks with impaired RNase P (tRNA-processing) function rather than the metabolic block.
Affected boys typically show initially normal development followed by regression, epilepsy, progressive choreoathetosis and dystonia, and loss of vision and hearing.
Additional features include cardiomyopathy, retinopathy and sensorineural hearing loss, reflecting a combined oxidative-phosphorylation defect.
The protein also metabolises neuroactive steroids such as allopregnanolone, and disturbed neurosteroid handling is proposed to contribute to neuronal injury.
Carrier females may be asymptomatic or symptomatic depending on skewed X-inactivation, so the diagnosis should not be dismissed in girls.
Isoleucine-pathway metabolites can be intermittent or near-normal, so molecular confirmation is definitive when clinical suspicion is high.
reference.pathophysiology: The HSD17B10 gene on the short arm of the X chromosome encodes a mitochondrial multifunctional protein. As an enzyme it catalyses an oxidation step in isoleucine degradation and participates in the breakdown of branched-chain fatty acids and neuroactive steroids; as MRPP2 it forms part of mitochondrial RNase P, the complex that cleaves the 5-prime ends of transfer RNAs from the polycistronic mitochondrial transcript. Pathogenic variants impair transfer RNA maturation, secondarily reducing synthesis of mitochondrial-DNA-encoded respiratory-chain subunits and producing a combined oxidative-phosphorylation defect. This failure of mitochondrial gene expression, rather than simple accumulation of isoleucine intermediates, is thought to drive the progressive encephalopathy, with disturbed neurosteroid metabolism and toxic build-up of 2-methyl-3-hydroxybutyryl-CoA as contributory mechanisms.
additionalDifferentials: Other Leigh-like mitochondrial encephalopathies from nuclear or mtDNA complex I/IV defects

additionalInvestigations: Plasma acylcarnitine profile (hydroxy-C5 and tiglyl species)
Plasma amino acids, with isoleucine provocation where diagnostically helpful
HSD17B10 sequencing with assessment of X-linked segregation
Blood and CSF lactate; respiratory-chain enzyme studies in muscle or fibroblasts
Brain MRI for basal ganglia and white-matter change and atrophy
Cardiac assessment (echocardiography, ECG), audiology and ophthalmology including electroretinography
redFlags: Developmental regression with new-onset seizures or a movement disorder in a boy
Rapidly progressive neurodegeneration with visual and hearing loss
Metabolic decompensation with acidosis during intercurrent illness
reference.prognosis: The neurodegenerative form is generally progressive with substantial disability and shortened life expectancy, whereas the rarer purely metabolic presentation may be milder; outcome does not reliably follow residual enzyme activity.
pitfalls: Misreading the organic-acid pattern as beta-ketothiolase deficiency; absence of 2-methylacetoacetate is the discriminator.
Assuming that near-normal enzyme activity or mild biochemistry excludes severe disease, when the RNase P defect drives prognosis.
Overlooking the diagnosis in females who can be symptomatic through skewed X-inactivation.
Expecting dietary isoleucine restriction to halt the neurodegenerative course.
Excluding the disorder prematurely when urine metabolites are intermittent or normal.
references: Inborn errors of metabolism reference texts
management: Consider mild isoleucine (protein) restriction, recognising that clinical benefit is limited because severity tracks the impaired mitochondrial tRNA processing rather than the metabolic block
Antiseizure medication for the epilepsy of the progressive encephalopathy
Pharmacotherapy for the movement disorder — agents for dystonia and choreoathetosis — combined with physiotherapy
Cardiac surveillance by echocardiography with heart-failure treatment for cardiomyopathy, and audiology and ophthalmology follow-up for sensorineural hearing loss and retinopathy
Supportive neurorehabilitation, sensory aids and nutritional support, with intravenous glucose during catabolic stress to limit decompensation
Coordinate care through metabolic medicine, neurology, cardiology and sensory specialists
Offer genetic counselling for X-linked inheritance with carrier testing of female relatives
